newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Clyde steps up bid defence.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Clyde steps up bid defence.

text.p: British bid target Clyde Petroleum attempted to prove on Tuesday that it was worth at least 62 million pounds ($100 million) more than Canada's Gulf Canada Resources's hostile offer.

In its final defence document, the oil exploration and production firm said an independent consultancy had valued its net assets between 120 and 144 pence per share compared with Gulf Canada's 105 pence offer.
It was the first time Clyde pointed at its net asset value to try to show that Gulf Canada's 432 million pounds offer was too low.
Market estimates on Clyde's net assets had ranged roughly between 70 and 80 pence per share.
But chairman Malcolm Gourlay said in a statement: "Now it is crystal clear quite how seriously Gulf Canada has undervalued Clyde's potential under its existing management team."
Clyde also announced a 21.7 percent increase in full-year earnings and forecast that its operating cash flow would grow by 18 percent to at least 150 million pounds in 1997.
Independent cash flow studies also implied that Clyde shares should be trading at at least 144 pence, Clyde said.

"Whether you use cash flow multiples or net asset values, Gulf Canada's offer comes nowhere near the value of Clyde's existing business let alone its future potential," said managing director Roy Franklin.
A Gulf Canada spokesman said the Canadian firm was preparing its response, which would probably be released later on Tuesday.
Gulf Canada Resources launched its hostile bid for Clyde on December 18. On Monday it extended it until February 4 after receiving acceptances for a mere 0.17 percent of Clyde's shares.

Shares in Clyde, which have consistently hovered well above Gulf Canada's offer, eased one pence to 117-1/2 pence, still reflecting lingering market hopes that a counter bidder will emerge to top Gulf Canada's offer.

Meanwhile, Clyde said it expected production to rise by nine percent to an average 44,900 barrels of oil equivalent per day (boepd) and increase further to an average 55,200 boepd in 1998 and 60,200 in 1999.

Earnings rose to 32.0 million pounds in 1996 from 26.3 million pound the previous year thanks to increased production and higher oil and gas prices. Clyde, which is mainly active in the North Sea, Australia and Indonesia, said it was looking for new venture opportunities in Australia after acquiring Crusader Ltd last year.

"Clyde's strategy is to increase production and reserves in order to sustain earnings and cash flow growth, through a balanced programme of acquisition, development and exploration," Clyde said in a statement accompanying its results. ($1=.6199 Pound)
